author: johnschulman2
text: Strange that "how does the brain implement backprop?"  doesn't get more attention in neurosci. (Some exceptions, e.g. Tim Lillicrap's work). I'm certain that the brain does it: (1) learning with gradients is much faster (2) backprop is the only efficient way to compute gradients

author: johnschulman2
text:
Glad to finally release this, as it includes a bunch of directions I'm excited about:
- RL with a reward function defined by human judgements
- language models using tools (a web browser)
- making it easier for humans to rate the AI's output (AI cites its sources)

author: johnschulman2
text: @gwern @NPCollapse I'd consider DT and any algo that uses a reward fn to be RL. Any algo that maximizes probability of high-reward trajectories will work. The algo you described will probably be less sample-efficient wrt human rankings than using a reward model as in the human prefs work

text: While studying classical piano, I briefly learned in music theory class about basso continuo, which is baroque-era improv over a bassline. That was fun, but I only really learned about chord progressions after I started playing jazz tunes out of a Real Book.

text: Kids who learned these skills would be more likely to keep them up later in life, rather than abandoning their instruments as soon as their parents stop schlepping them to music lessons.

author: johnschulman2
text: Musical training should put more emphasis on teaching chord changes and how to play over them instead of the motor skill of memorizing classical pieces. These skills are usually only taught with jazz, but they're useful for all genres.
